item.title: Carney says US trade war 'will come at a cost' as Canada strikes back on tariffs
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8jdev0422jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Carney says US trade war 'will come at a cost' as Canada strikes back on tariffs - Published Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that Canada's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost", as a wave of Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force. In a video address, Carney added that the counter-tariffs against the US "are necessary to protect our workers". Canada's levies will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of American products, from steel to furniture to cotton T-shirts, and will be as high as 50%. Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August. In Tuesday morning's 15-minute video address, Carney said his country's main focus was to diversify its trade relationships and build its economy. He added that his government would also support workers affected by the ongoing trade war with the US "for as long as it takes". "We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," the prime minister said. "That pivot will come at a cost. "There's always a cost to action, but it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still." US trade representative Jamieson Greer meanwhile said that Washington would consider imposing tit-for-tat tariffs on Canada as early as Tuesday. "We'll see this afternoon," he said in French, speaking to CBC News. President Donald Trump threatened on Monday to halt all US business with Canada-based airplane maker Bombardier unless it moved its manufacturing south. The aerospace giant is one of the largest in the country, contributing over C$7bn to Canada's annual GDP in 2024, according to a report by accounting firm PwC that was commissioned by Bombardier. Trump argues that these import taxes encourage consumers to buy American-made goods and boost investment in the US from foreign companies. But economists warn that prices rise for consumers on everyday goods that are targeted by tariffs. - What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans - Published3 hours ago - The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts - Published31 August - Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US - Published15 hours ago Trump took aim at Canada in a series of Truth Social posts over the weekend. Another post showed a map of North America - including Canada and Mexico - and Greenland all overlaid with the US flag. Canada and the US have the world's largest bilateral trading relationship valued at nearly $900bn last year. The US economy is about 13 times larger than Canada's, and the majority of Canadian exports are sold to the US. Businesses on both side of the border are scrambling to deal with what comes next. The US currently has in place a 25% tax on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as taxes on Canadian steel, aluminium and lumber. Golf clubs, cheese, toilet paper In late August, Trump imposed new 50% tariffs on other goods like dairy, alcohol, hockey sticks and perfume. Canada's counter-tariffs, which range from 15% to 50%, will from Tuesday be applied to hundreds of items coming in from the US. Products like American milk, golf clubs, steel, aluminium and jackets and T-shirts will face 50% tariffs. Cheese, toilet paper and certain household appliances like air conditioners will face 25% tariffs, while forklift trucks and industrial moulds will be hit with 15% tariffs. These levies are in addition to existing retaliatory taxes Canada placed on finished American cars and trucks that are not covered by a free trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada. Opinion polls suggest the majority of Canadians support, external their country imposing retaliatory tariffs on the US. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has urged the Carney government to take a surgical approach to retaliation. "Businesses understand retaliation but don't want to see endless escalation," the Chamber's CEO and President Candace Laing told the BBC on Friday. Pushback from the fisheries industry was enough for Canada to alter its counter-tariffs by removing dozens of seafood items to avoid unintended consequences to its own economy. The lobster industry in both Canada and the US is heavily dependent on the other, with American-caught lobster often sent north to be processed before it is shipped back to the US and sold. Ahead of the latest tariffs, Canada's economy had shown signs of resiliency. Its GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter and it had gained 181,000 jobs from April to July. But around 41,000 jobs were lost in August, a period that coincided with the new US tariffs on Canada and the collapse in trade talks. One sector that saw a modest bump was manufacturing - a gain the Canadian government attributes to consumers and businesses buying more made-in-Canada products. Data shows that Canada is also diversifying its trade. The share of US-bound Canadian exports dropped to 66% from an average of 75% before the trade war, according to July trade figures.

item.title: Four Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c70drp0pyw2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist - Published Four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France. Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on Tuesday morning but dropped two of the paintings in the institution's garden as they made their escape, local Mayor Bryan Masson said. The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight. One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen. CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said. The alarm went off at 05:48 (05:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms. He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed". They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added. Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects. The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered. The two paintings that are still missing are: - Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) - Jeune fille au puits (1886) And the two pieces that were recovered are: - Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895) - Coco Lisant (1905) "Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," the mayor told reporters at the museum. "It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," he said. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Last month, four Renaissance paintings being stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy. "Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," the local French mayor warned. Masson called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals". - Published16 August - Published20 October 2025

item.title: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8jd14glvneo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands - Published The Argentine government has said that it will file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands. The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean. Reacting to the news, Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill insisted that there could be "no doubt" about the British government's commitment to the Falkland Islanders. Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982. Speaking in the House of Commons on Tuesday, McNeill said that "the decision by the Falkland Islands government to pursue hydrocarbon production is a commercial decision for them to take alongside the commercial companies involved". She added that "the future of the Falkland Islands is for Falkland Islanders to determine". The simmering dispute between Britain and Argentina over the Falklands heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands. Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas. In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that." The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty. He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory. Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination". The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering". Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives. Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028. The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities. "The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted. Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development". Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands. Related topics - Published3 days ago

item.title: Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8m1k7p3v7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv - Published A Russian drone has struck a Ukrainian TV channel headquarters in Kyiv, injuring at least five people as journalists were broadcasting live, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Zelensky said the daytime attack was a "new page in Russian degradation", while photos shared by the president show a partially collapsed building. At least five people have been killed in overnight and daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv, while a separate attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine killed a female employee, officials have said. Both countries had earlier agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend. Referring to Tuesday's Russian drone attack on the Ukrainian TV channel We Are Ukraine, Zelensky said: "Today, Russia carried out a strike on the media, journalists. "Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts," he added in a renewed plea to Ukraine's allies in Europe, the US and around the world. Earlier on Tuesday, air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces carried out missile and drone strikes on Kyiv, the local authorities said. A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed three people and injured another 25, the state emergencies service DSNS said. Residential buildings were hit, including a five-storey house in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district. People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war. By Tuesday afternoon, the death toll had reached five people. According to a BBC Verify analysis, Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion. In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said early on Tuesday. The talks with Trump's top envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow and Kyiv ended without any major breakthroughs. Zelensky said he expected the war to continue into the winter, following the envoys' first visit to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. In Moscow, President Vladimir Putin's senior adviser Yuriy Ushakov said the US envoys were informed about "the significant advances made by the Russian armed forces" on the battlefield and stressed that the Kremlin's "set objectives would be achieved". Putin has so far showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine. Meanwhile, Witkoff said that "substantive progress was made", without giving any further details. Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US.

item.title: Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp849n2nz01o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities - Published Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has attacked energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia with dozens of drones and missiles, injuring 73 people, Saudi authorities say. Tuesday's attacks hit four south-western cities, causing fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that its forces would respond to the "dangerous escalation". The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi strikes on areas of north-western Yemen that they control. On Monday, they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of al-Hazm and killing at least 11 people. Twenty inmates are reportedly missing under the rubble. The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured. An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted. The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added. Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes". He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage". A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500. The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

item.title: Highest paid world leader to get salary increase of $1 million
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y5kn143d1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Highest paid world leader to get salary increase of $1 million - Published Singapore's government says it will raise the annual salaries of its ministers and other office holders, including its prime minister who is the highest paid political leader in the world. Lawrence Wong will see an increase of 1.4 million Singapore dollars ($1.1m; £818,000) in his annual pay package. He has said he will donate this pay increase to charity over the next five years. Wong said that raising the pay of ministers was necessary to attract better talent. The government has previously argued that paying ministers high salaries deters corruption. But the move has attracted criticism in Singapore where there is deep concern about job security and the rising cost of living. Even before his pay raise kicks in, Wong is still by far the highest paid world leader. He currently receives an annual salary of S$2.2m and will now see his pay go up by more than 60% to S$3.6m ($2.8m). Next is Hong Kong chief executive John Lee, who earns about $719,000, followed by Switzerland's president Guy Parmelin with $606,000. US president Donald Trump earns $400,000 a year, while British PM Andy Burnham takes in $230,000. On Tuesday, Wong acknowledged that Singapore ministers' salaries have attracted scrutiny given that they were much more than what most citizens earn. The median monthly income in the country is S$5,775. But he argued that he has faced difficulty convincing business leaders and top civil servants to run for political office. While the government cannot match what some of these people earn, "we do not make the financial hurdle unnecessarily high" for them to give up their careers and join politics, he said. "Overall, I believe this will give me and future prime ministers a better chance of persuading capable Singaporeans to step forward, and of building the strongest possible team for Singapore," he said. Currently, the base pay package of ministers is about S$1.1m. With the new pay scheme, that will increase to around S$1.2m. But Wong said he expects most of these ministers to receive even more than that - around S$1.35m - by the end of the current term of government, as pay will increase based on performance. Part of their pay package is determined by whether the country reaches certain targets for unemployment rate, income growth, and GDP growth. The topic of high salaries for Singapore's ministers has long been a lightning rod of criticism for the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has led the country since independence. In a landmark general election in 2011 the PAP saw its lowest vote share in decades, fuelled partly by voters' unhappiness over ministers' pay as well as immigration policies. The following year, the government slashed ministers' salaries. Wong's predecessor, Lee Hsien Loong, had also pledged to donate his salary increase to charity for several years back in 2007. The government has for years pointed to its lack of corruption - Singapore consistently ranks near the top of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index - as proof that the ministerial pay system works, arguing that it reduces the temptation for ministers to accept bribes. But in a country where the average income is far below such sums, the issue continues to rankle and the latest announcement is no exception. On Tuesday many online posted comments critical of the pay raise, saying it was "tone deaf" given current concerns about retrenchments, jobs for fresh graduates and inflation. Retrenchments in Singapore hit their highest level in more than five years in the last quarter, according to government figures. But there were a few who agreed with the move, saying it was necessary to have "the best of the best" running the country.

item.title: New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjdvyk3pm27o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani - Published Toxic air quality was being recorded in Manhattan soon after the 9/11 attacks, even as officials played down the health risks to the public, according to a trove of newly released files. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the 170,000 documents show asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" they tested near Ground Zero, the site where the World Trade Center towers collapsed in 2001. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," Mamdani said at a news conference with survivors. Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the collapse of the Twin Towers have claimed more lives than the attacks themselves, US health officials say. The document release resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued the city for the documents. City officials found 68 boxes of the documents last year. Officials had previously said they did not have them. "Administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity," Mamadani said, standing next to television host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart. "We will do no such thing." Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer from the terrorist attacks, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants from the building collapses. The pages of air quality reports and other documents were released through an online portal, timed with the 25th anniversary of the attacks. Mamdani said City Hall will spend more than $34m (£25m) on the effort. He said the documents show what the city "knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability". More documents are to be shared over the course of the next year. The release comes after years of survivors advocating for more transparency from city officials. Speaking at the news conference on Tuesday, Stewart said the documents show the city didn't recognise that the air that everyone was breathing in downtown Manhattan was toxic until October of 2001. "So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically. The documents include an October 2001 file known as the "Harding Memo", in which an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding - serving under Mayor Rudy Giuliani - that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks. The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)". Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe, though research suggests people were breathing in toxic chemicals. Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had". Elizabeth Cascio, a former New York Fire Department (FDNY) emergency medical technician, previously told the BBC that she suffered sinus issues and headaches after responding to the attacks. "We all knew the air quality was not safe – it was very toxic in terms of how it felt," she said. "Initially, when I came off the bus and arrived at the Trade Center, you felt like you had to hold your breath. But there's only so long you can hold your breath. I could feel the particles coming into my nose and mouth and thought: 'This can't be good'." Related topics - Published1 September 2011 - Published2 days ago

item.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddvzd1z53lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen - Published Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities. "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details. Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance. The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful". Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine. In May Anita Orbán summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022. Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger". Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita Orbán's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules". Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation". Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor Orbán objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia. Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked. Former Hungarian counter-intelligence chief András Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken. The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote. Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind. Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there."

item.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m8247yleo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns - Published Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned. Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said. MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action. The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance. MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance. According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year. - A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan - Published13 November 2025 - Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity - Published7 August "War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan. "MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours." This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment. "After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years. Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year. In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said. According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing. It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June. As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city. In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10. According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children. "If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said. At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said. In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide. According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger". The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war. Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex. item.title: Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyenxp540vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit - Published An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religious group. A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the iconic landmark in Paris on Saturday. "Women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated", staff union representative Diane Davoine said. The tower closed on Monday as staff went on strike to show their outrage. BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances. Ariel Weil, who is the president of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower, blamed its managers for being "a bit overzealous" in complying with the request without considering whether it was "inappropriate". Weil, who is also mayor of Paris Centre, told French broadcaster Franceinfo on Tuesday that the incident was "totally shocking and unacceptable". An internal investigation will determine who was responsible for putting the conditions in place, Weil said, and ensure it "never happens again". In a statement reported by AFP news agency, staff at the monument said that during Saturday's visit, female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present". "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so [on Monday morning], the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," Davoine said. Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), which runs the Eiffel Tower, had previously said the conditions imposed on female staff were not in line with its values "nor with the principles of equality between men and women". BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in a Parisian suburb. In a statement on X, BAPS said the trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others". It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service". On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values. It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney. It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation. BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory. Politicians in France have condemned Saturday's incident. Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors." French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'." Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

item.title: Five killed in Miami plane crash were in two vehicles on ground, investigators say
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8e32n8epeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Five killed in Miami plane crash were in two vehicles on ground, investigators say - Published The five people killed and five injured when an Amazon cargo plane crashed on landing at Miami International Airport were in two vehicles on the ground, investigators said. The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway on Sunday and hit an airline cleaning van holding seven people before breaking the perimeter fence and striking a Toyota SUV with three inside. Jennifer Homendy, chairwoman of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), called the crash scene "utter devastation" and said it was too early to identify a cause. Investigators have recovered the flight recorders and will look at flight systems, crew experience and weather as potential factors, say aviation experts. Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day. The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company. It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway. It was not clear from the NTSB's updates how many people died in each vehicle on the ground, or the condition of the two crew on board the plane. Debris from the aircraft, mangled vehicles and airport fencing was left strewn across the area. "It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," said Homendy during the press conference. She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait." The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation. Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene. Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing. The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation. Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots (48km/h). The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation. Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said. "Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again." Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash. Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews. The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US. Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities. The company operating the aircraft, 21 Air, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation. - Published1 day ago - Published22 hours ago

item.title: Trial over killing of Australian surfer brothers and US friend starts in Mexico

========================================
Trial over killing of Australian surfer brothers and US friend starts in Mexico - Published Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024. The bodies of Callum Robinson, his younger brother Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad from California - all in their early 30s - were found at the bottom of a well with gunshot wounds to their heads, days after they went missing during a surf trip in Baja California. Prosecutors are seeking jail sentences of more than 200 years for the defendants, who also face charges of violent robbery and auto theft. The parents of the brothers were in court on Tuesday in the coastal town of Ensenada, telling the media that it was "incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult". "We want the men accused of murdering our sons to see, in person, the human consequences of what happened," Martin and Debra Robinson said in a statement, according to Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC. "Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file - they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away." On the opening day, the accused - Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús - were moved to a smaller courtroom amid accusations that some witnesses had been intimidated by people associated with the defendants. Dozens of witnesses are expected to give evidence during the four-week, judge-only trial. The 2024 alleged killings of the Robinson brothers and their US friend shocked Australians as well as many residents of the normally peaceful town of Ensenada. Despite high levels of cartel violence in the northern Mexican border states, tourists are rarely targeted for such violent attacks in Baja California's surf towns. The ex-girlfriend of one of the accused, Ari Gisell, became the first person to be convicted over the tourists' killings last year and was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in their murders. Mexican prosecutors are pursuing jail sentences of more than 200 years for each of the defendants, as well as an additional 168-year sentence for the alleged ringleader. Prosecutors say the victims were killed due to a bungled robbery, while the defence argued there was not enough evidence to prove that theory. Callum Robinson was a member of Australia's national lacrosse team and lived in San Diego where he was a professional lacrosse player. His younger brother Jake had travelled from Australia for the surf trip and was due to start a job as a doctor when he returned while their friend Rhoad was killed a few months before his wedding. - Published9 May 2024 - Published7 May 2024 - Published6 May 2024

item.title: Kenya moves to register frightened Burundians as tension over foreign traders rises
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c158wwl22xko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Kenya moves to register frightened Burundians as tension over foreign traders rises - Published Kenya says it will register undocumented Burundians and other East Africans living in the country, following days of anxiety over President William Ruto's directive targeting foreigners in small-scale businesses. On Monday, hundreds of Burundians scrambled to process travel documents amid uncertainty over whether they could remain in Kenya. Charles Owino, the Kenyan government spokesperson, has now said those without proper documents should register through their embassies or high commissions as the authorities work with diplomatic missions to regularise their status. Those undergoing registration would be presumed legally in Kenya during the process, Owino said. Ruto had set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work. The directive came after the trade ministry said some foreigners exploit visa rules to work without the required permits. Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital, Nairobi, after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who wanted to go back home. Others were seen racing to buy bus tickets. Some Burundians have reportedly faced hostility after President Ruto ordered action against foreign street vendors and those operating small shops, saying such jobs should be protected for Kenyans. Kenyan officials have since sought to reassure neighbouring countries that there is no blanket ban on foreign traders. Addressing a news conference on Monday, Owino said the government had opened registration and documentation of all foreign nationals residing in Kenya without valid documents. He acknowledged that because of historical circumstances and regional dynamics, a number of East African nationals, including several Burundians, resided and operated in Kenya without full documentation. "To address this constructively, the government of Kenya is establishing a formal documentation and registration window," Owino said. "We call upon all undocumented East African community nationals, and specifically Burundian citizens currently residing in Kenya, to immediately present themselves to their respective high commissions or embassies for formal identity registration." In a statement on Tuesday, the Kenyan government said foreign nationals running businesses had 90 days to regularise their immigration status, work permits, business registrations and licences. After that the requirements would be "enforced firmly and strictly", it said. "During this period, the responsible government agencies will provide the necessary guidance and administer the applicable requirements fairly, consistently and without discrimination," Kenya State House's statement added. It also warned that no individual or group had "the authority to harass, intimidate, threaten or interfere with foreign nationals or their businesses". Senior Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'oei has apologised to Burundians over the harassment some have faced, saying the president's directive had been misunderstood. "I want to say sorry to all the Burundi nationals here," Sing'oei said during a visit to the Burundian embassy in Nairobi on Monday. He said the government would tighten security in areas where Burundians live. Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities. According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya. It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading. On Monday, some of them were seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they tried to leave Kenya. However, some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline. Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising anti‑migrant sentiment in South Africa. Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change". "Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added. Ruto had said that while Kenya remained open to foreign investment, it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop". He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses. His comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation. Bizimana organised an urgent meeting with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region. Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. He said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse. Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient. He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans were also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries. "This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda." Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police. item.title: Nepal cracks down on online abuse of flood survivors
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5x3n38308o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nepal cracks down on online abuse of flood survivors - Published Nepal is cracking down on online abuse directed at survivors of last month's deadly floods, with Prime Minister Balendra Shah warning that authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering. Some have taken to social media to appeal for information about their loved ones and to urge officials to step up search efforts, only to be hit by hostile comments. "People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals," Shah wrote in a Facebook post. Nepali police say they are looking into where these comments have originated from to identify addresses and phone numbers. A woman, whose brother has been missing since the floods hit two weeks ago, had earlier told the BBC that search and rescue operations were too slow. "If the government had mobilised experts and equipment for rescue in time, would we have known the condition of our family members sooner? "We still hope we can find him alive." Days later, she wrote back saying she had "received many nasty comments" in response to her criticism of the search efforts. "We are already suffering so much and this has only added to our pain," she said. In a separate case, a young woman had expressed her anger at what she perceived as authorities' "lack of urgency" in searching for her husband. "My husband is missing now, if the government cannot find him, can it at least show me his body?" she said in a video clip that has gone viral online – and attracted its fair share of insults. One comment, for instance, urged her to "jump into the river" and help with the search, while another read, "not everything happens just by you putting the blame on the government". But others have called out the insensitive remarks. "The victim should be consoled at this time, not cursed," one of them read. Nepali police say they have convened a 10-member committee to look into these online comments. Under the country's Electronic Transactions Act, those who use social media to defame or harass others could be jailed for up to five years and fined up to 100,000 rupees ($662; £490), or both. Dovan Rai, the executive director of Body & Data, a Nepal-based non-profit organisation that advocates for a safe digital space, says some of the insensitive comments could have come from social media users who engage in "rage baiting" – that is, those who produce negative content as a "bait" to trigger outrage, or force people to click on or share their posts. They could also have come from "staunch supporters of the government". "There is also extremism that is very sympathetic to the government and condemns those who question it. That has further polarized the dialogue on social media," she told the BBC.

item.title: North Korea and Russia open first road bridge linking both countries
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9xvg1kz0mo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
North Korea and Russia open first road bridge linking both countries - Published The first road bridge linking Russia and North Korea has opened, allowing the two countries to more easily move cargo and passengers between their border across the Tumen river. Pyongyang state media said the bridge will be used for "personnel exchanges, tourism and trade". But Ukrainian investigative organisation Truth Hounds said the bridge is intended "primarily to establish a covert military logistics corridor" to support Russia in the Ukraine war. It comes amid stronger ties between the countries since the start of the Ukraine war, with Russia's Putin and North Korea's Kim Jong Un previously pledging that they would help each other in the event of "aggression" against either country. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin described the bridge as a "new symbol of friendship", while North Korea's Prime Minister Pak Thae Song said it was a "historical event". Up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people can cross the bridge daily, Russian state news TASS reports. Satellite imagery reported by the BBC in May this year showed the kilometre-long bridge alongside several new access roads, a border checkpoint, support infrastructure and parking facilities. There are existing air links, as well as the rail link between the two countries, but until now the only road link was a makeshift solution where, by special arrangement, wooden planks were placed on the rail bridge to allow cars to travel over it, according to Reuters. The Russian government said the bridge will initially be used to transport cargo, Reuters reported, before opening to passenger traffic later this year. The bridge would provide, a "powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," said Mishustin. Appearing at the opening ceremony via video link, he described ties between Moscow and Pyongyang as being "at an unprecedented high level." The most immediate impact may be increased export of weapons to Russia. Researchers at South Korea's spy agency estimates that North Korea has already transferred $7 to 14 billion dollars' worth of rockets, missiles, artillery shells using ships. An estimated 11,000 North Korean troops are actively fighting Ukrainians in Russia. Truth Hounds said in a recent statement that given the strategic partnership treaty between the two countries in 2024 - the bridge could be used to transport North Korean military personnel, construction workers and senior military officials directly to Russia. It would also enable the flow of Russian technology and resources in the opposite direction". Construction started in 2025, after the agreement to build the bridge was made during Putin's 2024 visit to North Korea, his first trip to the state in 24 years, which resulted in the partnership treaty. The bridge took 495 days to complete, after delays. Russian tourists have trickled into North Korea since they were allowed in in 2024. North Korea has been hosting them in capital Pyongyang and the beach resorts of Wonsan-Kalma, while continuing to block those from other countries. The road is also expected to transport North Korean labourers to Russia. Around 10,000 North Koreans are working in Russia's construction sites and logging camps, according to a South Korean estimate. Although the UN bans countries from using North Korean labour, many enter Russia under the guise of student visas. "The speed of construction is a reflection of the volume of trade activity between the two sides," Victor Cha from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank, told BBC Verify in May this year. "This is spurred largely by North Korea's provision of troops, weapons, munitions, and labourers for Putin's war in Ukraine," he said. "It is fair to say that this connection, prior to the war in Ukraine, was one of the sleepiest links between North Korea and its two neighbours." Related topics - Published12 August 2025

item.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj8xx5010o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US - Published President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there. "NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank'." The move came amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs were imposed on $20bn (£14.7bn) of US goods. In a statement, Bombardier said it employed thousands of American workers and that it valued its partnerships with US companies. The BBC has reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney's office for comment. It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US. The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers. It also operates sites in Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, DC and New Jersey. About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US. In a statement on Monday, Bombardier did not address Trump's threat directly, but said its operations "create tens of thousands of US jobs through the company's growing American footprint". "Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees," its statement said. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country." Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US. The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier. It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector. In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy". She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support. On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation." "Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market." Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied. item.title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy6gd228vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers - Published Juicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank. This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law. The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries. Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements. Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's foreign minister called it "hostile" and announced a series of counter measures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting". Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods. "As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets." West Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution. At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high". With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities. In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years. Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant". Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported. In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful". As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories". "I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets." Medjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley. "These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho. Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive. Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank. Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs. Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs. The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure. This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK. Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth. "Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says. "They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land." Israeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders. Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital. However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s. Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians. There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now. Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes. There have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced. A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders. However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned. "A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says. "I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely." Israel's Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, responded quickly to the UK's announcement, branding the move "morally distorted" and constituting a "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process", referring to Israel's general election in late October. He announced "a series of Israeli countermeasures", including the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and the removal of British representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) in Kiryat Gat, which is in charge of co-ordinating the shaky ceasefire in the Gaza Strip. "The message to every government that harms us is clear: whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region," Saar warned. Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch diplomats from the IGSC, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements. Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium. Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel. - Published18 hours ago - Published28 August

item.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
item.description:

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why? - Published The images are hard to ignore. Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation. One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra. They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state. At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner. Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation. His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products. "These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC. The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant. Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity. But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him. An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it. "I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC. Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives. In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions. "When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language. But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet. The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is. Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled. And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive. By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000. Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said. "Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible". Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public. The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram. However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic. Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed". Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons. "While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association. Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first. His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach. In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law. The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard". The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses? Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations. For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone. "Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC. He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety. "We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption." The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work. Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes. Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools. But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post. "The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal. The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds. For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets. Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban. "We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

item.title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
